newsitem.title: USA: Alaskan fires grow after rain gives brief respite.
newsitem.headline: Alaskan fires grow after rain gives brief respite.

text.p: Vast Alaskan wildfires, held in check over the weekend by long-awaited rain showers, continued to grow once the rain stopped, officials said Monday.
Three hundred forty firefighters were battling the edge of a 480,000-acre blaze that threatened three Athabaskan Indian villages along the Kuskokwim River, officials said.
That blaze, named the Inowak Fire, has not grown significantly since the weekend, the Alaska Interagency Coordination Centre, the federal and state office managing wildfires, said.

Residents of all three villages -- Sleetmute, Red Devil and Stony River -- have been on alert for weeks for possible evacuation from the lightning-sparked wildfire. A community meeting was scheduled for Stony River Monday night, the centre said.

Two firefighting crews were trying to protect cabins at the southern perimeter of large wildfires in the Innoko National Wildlife Refuge, the interagency centre said. Together, those fires covered 607,000 acres, the centre said.
In all, 87 wildfires were burning statewide Monday, most in areas not designated for fire suppression.

So far this summer, 632 fires have burned more than 1,458 million acres statewide, the centre said. That is the largest total acreage burned in Alaska since 1991. State and federal officials have cited hot, dry weather as the reason for the spread of lightning-sparked blazes.
The Alaska Interagency Coordination Centre combines fire management efforts of the Alaska Division of Forestry and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management.
